chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, from Ayub ibn Nuh, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Abu Usamah al-Shahham, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A relative or brother-in-law of mine swore an oath: 'If his wife exits the door, she is divorced three times.' She exited, and her husband had intercourse with her as much as Allah willed, causing her hardship. He ordered me to ask you. He leaned towards me and said, 'Tell him to keep her; it is nothing.'
Then he turned to the people and said, 'Glory be to Allah, they order her to marry while she has a husband.'

And whoever divorces his wife and is contrary [to the conditions] and does not fulfill the conditions of divorce, except that he believes that separation occurs through it, this is binding upon him. What indicates this is what was narrated: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamadani, who said: I wrote to Abu Ja'far al-Thani (peace be upon him) along with some of our companions, and the answer came to me in his handwriting: 'I understood what you mentioned regarding your daughter and her husband. May Allah rectify for you what you love to be rectified. As for what you mentioned regarding his sinning by divorcing her more than once, look (carefully), may Allah have mercy on you. If he is among those who follow us and say with our saying, there is no divorce upon him because he did not do something he was ignorant of. And if he is among those who do not follow us and do not say with our saying, then effect a khul' (divorce by redemption) for her from him, for he only intended separation with his own self.'

key_terms.حِنْثٌ: Sin or breaking of an oath

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a conditional divorce oath where the condition is met but the husband does not intend to separate?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the concept of *Talaq al-Mu'allaq* (conditional divorce), distinguishing between the literal fulfillment of the condition and the husband's underlying intent (*niyyah*). The Imam emphasizes that for those adhering to Shia jurisprudence, such divorces are often treated as non-binding or simple due to ignorance of the precise legal mechanism, whereas for others, it may necessitate *Khul'* (divorce by redemption). This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on intent and the flexibility of divorce rulings when the condition is merely a formality rather than a desire for permanent separation. Additionally, the text notes that if the divorce conditions are not fully met but the husband believes it is effective, the separation still stands, illustrating the principle of *I'tiqad* (conviction) in legal outcomes.
